paragraphs: Scope: this page covers only O*NET-SOC 51-9195.00, Molders, Shapers, and Casters, Except Metal and Plastic, for career exploration. It excludes more specific occupations such as metal and plastic casting, custom glassblowing, stone carving, and pottery making, and does not authorize operation or safety work involving molds, heating equipment, hot work, or lifting.

How to assess: use entirely fictional product specifications and a formula table to check whether you can sequence mold selection, ingredient preparation and mixing, pouring and compaction, curing temperature and time, demolding and finishing, and dimensional review, and describe three checkpoints and anomaly responses. Perform paper exercises only, without real kilns, molds, or hot materials.

Who it suits: people willing to weigh and mix precisely according to formulas, repeatedly verify molds and temperatures, notice surface and dimensional deviations, remain steady during prolonged standing and repetitive movements, and stop to seek verification when materials or equipment are uncertain. These are behavioral signals, not personality diagnoses.

Note: personality labels and interest codes cannot determine fit or qualifications. Exercises on this page do not authorize equipment operation, hot work, dust-exposed work, or lifting and do not use real molds, employer formulas, or production data.

The official scope of molders, shapers, and casters, except metal and plastic (O*NET-SOC 51-9195.00) is molding, shaping, forming, casting, or carving products such as food, figurines, tiles, pipes, and candles from clay, glass, plaster, concrete, stone, or combinations of these materials. Excludes more specific occupations such as metal and plastic casting, custom glassblowing, stone carving, and pottery making.

entries: Work order interpretation and mold selection: read work orders or inspect workpieces to determine parts or sections to produce, and select mold sizes and types according to instructions.
Ingredient preparation and mixing: weigh materials according to formulas and mix molding materials, casting materials, or sealants to specified consistencies.
Mold preparation: clean, finish, and lubricate molds and mold parts, brush or spray release agents onto mold surfaces, and insert wires, pipe fittings, cores, inserts, or templates.
Pouring and compaction: pour, pack, spread, or press plaster, concrete, or other materials into models and molds, tapping or tilting them to distribute materials evenly.

Curing and drying control: set operating temperatures for each pour, operate heating equipment to melt materials or cure, dry, or bake filled molds, and load or stack molds in ovens, dryers, curing boxes, racks, or carts.

Demolding and finishing: remove cores or loosen mold parts after castings solidify, separate models and molds, trim or remove excess material, repair broken edges and cracks using clay or plaster, and grind mold surfaces.

Dimensional and appearance review: verify product dimensions using calipers, vernier instruments, or protractors, measure and cut to specified sizes, inspect accuracy, document mold numbers, formulas, temperatures, and measured values, and hand over.

paragraphs: Work context (O*NET Work Context survey): 99% of respondents wear common protective or safety equipment daily, 94% stand continually or almost continually, 90% continually use their hands to operate tools and materials, 82% perform repetitive motions, 79% encounter distracting noise, 76% work indoors in conditions that are not environmentally controlled, 68% encounter contaminants, gases, dust, or odors, and 57% are exposed to temperatures above approximately 32°C or below 0°C.

Capability priorities: understand work orders and mold specifications, accurately weigh and mix according to formulas, control pouring and curing temperatures, review products against dimensional and appearance standards, and stop to seek verification when materials are abnormal, temperatures are uncontrolled, or equipment is uncertain. Requires materials, mold, and hot-work knowledge and procedural recordkeeping habits.

Occupational judgments: key decisions concern mold-material compatibility, ingredient concentration and pouring quantity, compliance of curing temperatures and times, and conformity of product dimensions and appearance. Stop equipment and escalate first when uncertain or beyond authorization.

Main outputs: conforming shaped products such as food, figurines, tiles, pipes, and candles; traceable mold and formula records; temperature and time records; and dimensional and appearance review results.

Complete work cycle: work order interpretation and mold selection, mold preparation, ingredient preparation and mixing, pouring and compaction, curing and drying control, demolding and finishing, dimensional and appearance review, and records and handover. Each step requires verifiable evidence.

Choose directions based on actual tasks and verifiable evidence. This occupation centers on shaping nonmetallic materials using molds; casting workers focus on molten metal or plastic and casting equipment, glassblowers on hot glass shaping, stone cutters and carvers on subtractive processing, and modelmakers on making verifiable working models from drawings.

Comparisons use official O*NET 51-9195.00 and adjacent occupation task and industry descriptions. Similar titles do not make materials, processes, qualifications, and safety authorizations interchangeable.

Adjacent directions support comparisons of materials, forming methods, outputs, and responsibility boundaries only, not job recommendations. Check individually who selects molds, prepares ingredients, controls temperatures, and judges dimensional and appearance conformity.

Difference from Molding, Coremaking, and Casting Machine Setters, Operators, and Tenders, Metal and Plastic: those workers operate metal or plastic molding, coremaking, and pouring equipment, handling melts and molding machines. This occupation primarily molds, shapes, and carves nonmetallic materials such as clay, glass, plaster, concrete, and stone.

If you prefer shaping hot glass, compare glassblowing; if you prefer subtractive carving and cutting, compare stone cutting and carving; if you prefer making verifiable working models from drawings, compare modelmaking.
Current forming workers
Use tools for mold and ingredient checklist organization, ingredient conversions, and temperature record organization, retaining human review, first-article confirmation, and shutdown for anomalies.
Apprentices and newcomers

First practice mold selection, ingredient preparation, and measuring instrument use, then use controlled tools to organize work orders and ingredient records. Complete tabletop verification before handling heating equipment.
Team and process personnel
Include formula versions, mold numbers, curing curves, and first-article decisions in review points. Handle anomalies according to shutdown and escalation rules and retain audit trails.
Career changers
Develop material and mold fundamentals first, then accumulate products and process records through public or simulated projects. Do not treat generated content as capability evidence.

Insufficient evidence: mainland Chinese national occupational wages matching 51-9195.00 have not been obtained. NBS2025 manufacturing and production/manufacturing group averages are related references only, not occupational or individual wages.

In 2025, average annual wages of manufacturing employees in mainland China's urban non-private units were 113,594 yuan/year (National Bureau of Statistics definition, nominal growth 5.2%). This is an industry proxy, not exact occupational wages.

In 2025, manufacturing average annual wages in urban private units were 76,055 yuan/year (nominal growth 6.4%); production, manufacturing, and related personnel in enterprises above designated size earned 80,739 yuan/year (nominal growth 2.8%). Different statistical populations cannot be combined into a range.

In mainland China, this occupation may correspond to building material and concrete product, ceramic and glass product, craft product, and food forming roles. Actual compensation also depends on region, materials and process types, shifts, and experience. Check published conditions for specific cities, employers, and job levels.

National Bureau of Statistics wage coverage includes urban legal entities with 5 or more employees, excluding individual businesses and freelancers. U.S. O*NET/BLS figures cannot be converted or extrapolated across jurisdictions into individual earnings in mainland China.

This checklist is an editorial synthesis and cannot replace employer safety procedures, heating equipment and kiln operating procedures, or local regulations. Specific protection, exposure limits, and authorization depend on relevant authority and employer documents.

The main issues to assess in advance are dust and skin contact, burns from hot materials and heating equipment, strain from prolonged standing and repetitive movements, and batch scrap from ingredient, temperature, or measurement errors. Exposure points differ across molds and hand shaping, kiln and drying control, and review and delivery.

Evidence scope: dust and respiratory health references U.S. CDC/NIOSH silica and occupational health materials; machine and heating equipment guarding references relevant U.S. OSHA 29 CFR 1910 standards. Work context percentages reflect U.S. O*NET respondents and are not extrapolated to other regions.
Affected roles and tasks: personnel mixing, grinding, and finishing surfaces while exposed to plaster, concrete, and stone dust.

Dust exposure from materials containing respirable crystalline silica is associated with silicosis, lung cancer, COPD, and kidney disease. Not all dust, such as plaster dust, should be treated as silica dust.

ai_impact_table.responsibility_intro: The following steps describe the sequence of human controls when this occupation uses tools: input verification, conditions of use, output review, and recordkeeping.

responsibility_steps.说明: Verify work orders, mold numbers, material batches, and formula versions, confirming clear requirements and usable sources.
Begin forming only when formula and mold versions are controlled and material and equipment conditions are met.
People review pouring and compaction results, curing curves, and first-article dimensions and appearance rather than directly accepting tool outputs.
Record mold numbers, formulas, temperatures and times, measured dimensions, and rework decisions, retaining versions and deviations.
Stop and escalate to the responsible person when work exceeds scope or authorization or results are uncertain.

risk_rows.为什么重要: Will cause entire batches to be scrapped and reworked
risk_rows.控制方式: Verify mold numbers, formula versions, and material batches before starting; begin batch forming only after first-article confirmation

risk_rows.为什么重要: Products develop voids, missing material, or inadequate strength
risk_rows.控制方式: Verify ingredient quantities and compaction methods against process standards. Process and quality personnel determine first-article testing methods; destructive sectioning is not universally required.

risk_rows.为什么重要: Products crack, deform, or fail to cure
risk_rows.控制方式: Set temperatures by material and record curves; immediately stop equipment and respond procedurally to overtemperature

risk_rows.为什么重要: Prolonged contact with plaster, concrete, and stone dust is associated with skin and respiratory health risks
risk_rows.控制方式: Ventilation and wet methods, enclosed conveying, and suitable respiratory and skin protection

risk_rows.为什么重要: Cannot establish dimensional and appearance conformity or trace batches
risk_rows.控制方式: Reinspect according to instrument and recordkeeping standards; retain mold numbers, formulas, temperatures, and measured values

risks.mitigation: Prioritize low-silica materials and wet methods, combined with ventilation, enclosed conveying, suitable respiratory protection, and exposure monitoring
risks.scenario: Dust rises during cutting, grinding, or mixing stone, concrete, and other materials containing crystalline silica. Verify material composition first; plaster dust is not automatically silica dust.
risks.title: Silica dust and dust exposure

risks.affected_roles: Personnel pouring, loading and unloading ovens, and removing demolded pieces
risks.consequence: May cause skin scalds and burns and delay batches through downtime
risks.mitigation: Use fixtures and thermal protection, follow cooling and oven-opening procedures, provide warnings and interlocks, and receive hot-work training
risks.scenario: Contact with molten or hot materials, molds, ovens, and curing boxes, or opening ovens and retrieving pieces contrary to procedures
risks.title: Burns from hot materials and heating equipment

risks.affected_roles: Personnel mixing, pouring, demolding, and cleaning
risks.consequence: O*NET shows contaminant exposure context. Insufficient evidence: specific skin/respiratory health assessments for each material and release agent used have not been obtained; check SDS.
risks.mitigation: Use gloves and aprons, wash promptly, provide ventilation and local exhaust, and use chemicals according to safety data sheets
risks.scenario: Prolonged skin contact with cement, plaster, clay, or release agents without washing and protection
risks.title: Skin and respiratory irritation

risks.affected_roles: Personnel preparing ingredients, pouring, and reviewing
risks.consequence: May require entire batches to be scrapped or reworked and affect delivery and acceptance
risks.mitigation: Confirm first articles, check molds, document formulas and temperatures, and reinspect using instruments before batch production
risks.scenario: Mold wear or misread specifications, ingredient concentration deviations, or unsuitable curing temperatures cause cracks, deformation, or missing material
risks.title: Out-of-tolerance dimensions and appearance and rework

risks.affected_roles: Personnel pouring, handling materials, and finishing surfaces
risks.consequence: Repeated standing, hand use, and movements are official context. Editorial suggestion: assess loads. Body-part strain incidence or causal studies for this occupation have not been obtained.
risks.mitigation: Rotate tasks, use handling aids and adjustable work surfaces, and schedule appropriate breaks and stretching
risks.scenario: Prolonged standing, repeated handling, and repetitive movements with substantial shift demands
risks.title: Repetitive movements and physical strain

risks.affected_roles: Personnel responsible for process records and handovers
risks.consequence: Difficult to establish conformity or trace batches, increasing rework and claim risks
risks.mitigation: Record mold, formula, temperature, and measurement data according to standards and retain versions and deviations
risks.scenario: Failing to record mold numbers, formulas, temperatures, and measured dimensions or document rework decisions
risks.title: Incomplete batch and process records

description.text: Molders, shapers, and casters, except metal and plastic (O*NET 51-9195.00), mold, shape, and carve products from clay, glass, plaster, concrete, and stone. This page explains official tasks and work context, the U.S. BLS 2025 median wage of 46,170 USD and 6% growth for 2024—2034, mainland Chinese manufacturing and broad production/manufacturing job category proxy wages, AI task boundaries, fit signals, and entry paths.

title.text: Molders, shapers, and casters, except metal and plastic

subject.name: Molders, shapers, and casters, except metal and plastic
subject.summary: Molders, shapers, and casters, except metal and plastic (O*NET 51-9195.00), mold, shape, form, cast, or carve products such as food, figurines, tiles, pipes, and candles from clay, glass, plaster, concrete, stone, or combinations of these materials. Work centers on work order and mold checks, ingredient mixing, pouring and compaction, curing and drying temperature control, demolding and finishing, and dimensional and appearance review.
